content: Horchata, also known as orxata, refers to a variety of plant-based beverages that are traditionally made from ground almonds, rice, barley, or tiger nuts (chufas). The term horchata originates from the Valencian word orxata, which is likely derived from the Latin term hordeata, meaning made from barley (hordeum). While the French orgeat, the Italian orzata, and the Surinamese Dutch orgeade share the same linguistic root, the beverages themselves have evolved over time and are no longer typically made from barley. According to a popular legend, King James I of Aragon was offered a glass of horchata by an Arab girl after his conquest of Valencia. Upon tasting it, he is said to have exclaimed, Això és or, xata. which translates to This is gold, girl. In Spain, horchata most commonly refers to orxata de xufes (horchata de chufas), a drink made from tiger nuts, water, and sugar. This beverage, which originated in Valencia, is traditionally served ice-cold as a refreshing drink. A regulatory council oversees the quality of horchata and designates specific villages where it can be produced under the Denomination of Origin. The village of Alboraya is particularly renowned for its high-quality horchata. The practice of making horchata from tiger nuts dates back to the period of Muslim rule in Valencia, which lasted from the 8th to the 13th century. In Latin America, horchata varies significantly by region. In some countries, the drink is typically tan and milky in appearance, with recipes that may or may not include milk. Common ingredients include sugar, cinnamon, and vanilla. While horchata was traditionally homemade, it is now widely available in grocery stores in both ready-to-drink (shelf-stable or refrigerated) and powdered forms. In the United States, rice-based horchata, also known as morro horchata, is commonly served in Mexican restaurants, whereas horchata de chufas is virtually unknown. Rice-based horchata can also be found in grocery and convenience stores, particularly in Latino neighborhoods. In Mexican cuisine, horchata is one of the three classic flavors of aguas frescas, alongside tamarindo and jamaica. In El Salvador, horchata is often made from a blend of herbs rather than rice. It is typically flavored with morro (calabash tree) seeds, ground cocoa, cinnamon, sesame seeds, and sometimes strained for a smoother texture. In Nicaragua and Honduras, horchata refers to a drink known as semilla de jicaro, which is made from ground jicaro seeds mixed with rice and spices. This version is prepared with cold milk and sugar and is highly popular throughout the region. Recently, Nicaragua has begun exporting this product, primarily to the United States. Horchata is also used as a mixer in alcoholic beverages. In some Latin-American bars in Southern California, it is featured in a cocktail called the Rice Rocket. This drink consists of two parts horchata, one part coconut-flavored rum, and a dash of Goldschläger, served over ice.
